header: Date: 2025-05-20 15:00 PDT; Duration: ~62m; Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Infra), Carlos Mendes (CTO, Atlas Health), Aisha Khan (ML Eng), Lena Wu (Platform), Ben Ortiz (Security)
summary: Deep technical session focused on running models with 128k+ context at production scale. Covered long-context attention strategies, KV cache management, batching and latency trade-offs, quantization impact on throughput/accuracy, and VPC/on-prem nuances. Customer wants a pilot for radiology notes search + summarization with 128k windows, strict data residency, and SOC2 compliance. Agreed next steps: share benchmarks and run customer-sample microbenchmarks; Redwood to propose Dedicated pilot config and pricing.
topics: Attention optimizations (sparse/flash/linformer-like techniques and kernel selection)
Batching, continuous batching, and latency SLOs
Quantization (4-bit GPTQ/AWQ trade-offs) and performance regression risks
VPC/on-prem deployment considerations, KMS, data residency
transcript: [00:00] Jordan Lee: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood here — I'm the AE on this account. We've got Priya and Ethan with me. How are you all?

[00:08] Carlos Mendes: Hey Jordan, good — Carlos here. We set aside an hour to go deep on long context. We've got a couple of goals: understand performance with 128k windows, how KV caching behaves, and what the dedicated/pilot path looks like from a security perspective.

[00:25] Priya Raman: Awesome. We'll kick off with how we approach very long contexts in the runtime, then dive into KV cache, batching, and quant. We'll also hit VPC/on-prem hooks at the end. Quick callout: some of the numbers are from internal bench runs; we'll share the spreadsheet after.

[00:40] Aisha Khan: Quick note: our use case is clinical document search + summarization across patient history, many docs per patient — so 100k+ tokens is common. Latency target is ~1.2s for a single-shot summarize? But we can tolerate up to 5s if throughput is better. Cost needs to be predictable.
[00:55] Lena Wu: And infra constraints — we need VPC peering, zero public internet egress for PHI, KMS in our region, and SOC2 aligned logging.

[01:10] Jordan Lee: That's helpful. High level: our Dedicated offering can give you reserved GPU pools, private control plane options for VPC, and we have KMS integrations. For the long context specifics, Priya take it away.

[01:20] Priya Raman: Sure. At a runtime level, there are a few levers for 128k+: 1) chunking input into overlapping windows with smart retrieval; 2) KV cache with multi-tier storage; 3) attention kernel selection — e.g., FlashAttention for dense blocks and custom kernels for very long sparsity patterns; 4) sharded KV across GPUs when sequence length outgrows a single device's memory.
[01:45] Ben Ortiz: Sorry, can you explain the multi-tier KV cache? We think of cache as in memory only.

[01:49] Priya Raman: Yeah — multi-tier is a design we've used: a hot in-GPU LRU KV cache for very recent tokens, a warm host RAM cache, and an on-disk serialized layer for older prefixes. When you hit the on-disk tier, we can stream the required KV pages back into host RAM and then refill to GPU as needed. It avoids re-computing attention for far prefixes but does add some IO latency if you cold-load pages.
[02:10] Carlos Mendes: So for a 128k prompt, does Redwood keep the entire KV in GPU memory? Seems impractical.

[02:14] Priya Raman: Correct — typically we do sharding across devices and evict older context to host/disk. For 128k it depends on model size and kv-dtype. With 16-bit KV we'd need more memory; with 8-bit/4-bit store we can compress, but that affects precision. We usually recommend a hybrid: keep the most recent N tokens hot on GPU, stream older chunks when needed, and use prefix indices to avoid full-scans.
[02:35] Carlos Mendes: Makes sense. What about attention optimizations — are you doing sparse attention or some approximate methods? We worry about hallucination from weird attention approximations.

[02:42] Priya Raman: We don't blindly apply approximations. Our runtime selects kernels per attention pattern: dense FlashAttention for contiguous windows, block-sparse for chunked retrieval, and for retrieval-augmented generation we rely on chunking + rerank to keep the model operating in dense mode for the relevant tokens. For absolutely huge contexts we also have a 'sliding window with global tokens' approach — keep global summary tokens that represent document state — that reduces computation while preserving signal.
[03:05] Aisha Khan: Sliding window + global tokens — curious how you generate and update global tokens without drift.

[03:10] Priya Raman: Good question. It's an engineering tradeoff: we periodically recompute global tokens during off-peak or async summarization. For streaming, we update incrementally with attention to drift; we also include a confidence score. For clinical apps you'd likely set stricter refresh cadence.
[03:25] Speaker 6: (inaudible) — is there a public paper on the global token approach or is that Redwood internal?
[03:29] Priya Raman: Mostly internal engineering patterns, but inspired by recent long-context model papers. We'll include references in the follow-up notes.
[03:40] Jordan Lee: Let's talk batching: customer wants low latency for single requests but throughput for bulk operations. Priya, how does continuous batching handle 1.2s SLOs vs throughput?

[03:48] Priya Raman: Continuous batching tries to aggregate concurrent requests for better GPU utilization without violating latency SLOs. You can set a max wait (e.g., 20ms) or an SLO-driven policy: if the queue time threatens 1.2s, we flush early. For very long-context calls, batching is trickier because memory usage per request is high. We often do length-aware batching — group by similar context length — and adaptive batching that trades off latency for cost.
[04:15] Lena Wu: Length-aware batching sounds neat. Does that require the client to send declared length ahead of time?
[04:20] Priya Raman: We infer length from the request metadata or tokenized prefix. A small pre-flight tokenization step is cheap and helps the router pick a batch slot with similar lengths.
[04:30] Aisha Khan: Quantization — we were hoping to run 4-bit models to save cost. Concerned about quality drop, especially with medical terms. What's your experience?

[04:36] Priya Raman: Short answer: GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit can be good but you must validate on your domain prompts. We run evals across prompt sets and don't recommend blind rollouts. In our 128k bench, 4-bit model variants reduced memory footprint by ~2.5x and improved tokens/sec, but we saw small regressions in named-entity recall on clinical utterances in some cases. For those, mixed precision or 8-bit is safer.
[05:00] Carlos Mendes: Can we do a per-model A/B test in pilot? E.g., default to 8-bit and run background evals on 4-bit to compare?
[05:05] Priya Raman: Absolutely — rollouts with canary and A/B test are standard. Redwood Optimize can run quality monitors and regression alerts tied to your evaluation sets.

[05:20] Ethan Park: On deployment side, for Dedicated or Private, the key is control plane vs data plane separation. For VPC/on-prem, we can deploy the data plane in your VPC (or on-prem) and keep control plane interactions minimal — all metrics, logs, and model artifacts can be pushed over peered connectivity. KMS calls can be routed to your KMS endpoint.
[05:40] Ben Ortiz: On audit: we need immutable audit logs for token-level access, and field-level redaction for PHI in logs. Do you support that?
[05:46] Jordan Lee: Yes — we can configure log redaction and persistent audit trails in Dedicated/Private. We'll include SOC2 and audit detail links.
[06:00] Aisha Khan: Back to KV cache eviction: what eviction policy do you recommend for our workload (many docs, but queries focused on recent visits)?

[06:06] Priya Raman: LRU with semantic weighting usually works — weight tokens from recent encounters higher, and expire older patient history less aggressively if flagged as high-importance. We also support pinning specific prefixes (e.g., critical patient summary) to always keep hot.
[06:20] Carlos Mendes: Does pinning increase cost dramatically?
[06:24] Priya Raman: It increases memory usage but reduces compute rework. For a small set of pinned prefixes it's a net win; you can control pin size via policy.
[06:30] Speaker 6: (crosstalk) also latency distribution — do you have p95/p99s from your 128k bench?
[06:35] Jordan Lee: Yes — Priya, do you want to call out the bench numbers?

[06:38] Priya Raman: From our internal 128k sim on a 4xA100 reserved cluster running a 30B model: cold-load p95 was ~4.8s and p99 ~9.2s when restoring from disk to GPU; warm GPU-hot p95 was ~0.9s and p99 ~1.6s. With 4-bit quant we saw improvement in tokens/sec and slightly lower p95, but as I mentioned there were occasional recall regressions on medical entities. We'll share the raw CSV. Note these are synthetic — customer samples can vary.
[07:05] Aisha Khan: Those cold p99s are high but acceptable if it's rare. Can the runtime pre-warm KV based on patient ID?

[07:12] Priya Raman: Yes, pre-warm hooks exist. If you pass a stable patient identifier, the router can proactively load pinned segments or hot pages before the request arrives — requires some telemetry from your side but reduces cold starts substantially.
[07:26] Lena Wu: For VPC, how do you handle software updates/patching for on-prem nodes? We need patch windows and an approval flow.

[07:32] Ethan Park: For Private deployments, patching is done via images we push through your air-gapped channel or on a staged upgrade plan. We support maintenance windows and can provide a change log and rollback image.
[07:44] Ben Ortiz: KMS integration — do you support HSM-backed keys?
[07:47] Priya Raman: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM — AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSMs via KMIP. We can sign attestations for key usage.
[07:55] Carlos Mendes: One more on quant: if a 4-bit variant regresses on some metrics, do you keep it as fallback or do you prefer model variant fallback?

[08:02] Priya Raman: We build fallback policies — you can route high-risk queries to a higher-precision variant (8-bit or FP16) automatically when the quality monitor score is low or when certain triggers fire (e.g., medical entity detected). That way you still get cost savings for the bulk while protecting critical queries.
[08:18] Aisha Khan: Good — can we see how Redwood's monitoring reports entity-level regressions?
[08:23] Jordan Lee: We'll include a demo of the Optimize dashboards in the follow-up, with example regressions and alerts.
[08:34] Speaker 6: (soft) — about kernel selection — do you manually choose kernel per model or is it automatic?

[08:38] Priya Raman: Kernel selection is automatic in the runtime. We have a heuristics engine plus offline profiling that picks the best kernel for a given model, sequence length, and hardware. You can override if needed, but defaults work well for most cases.
[08:55] Carlos Mendes: Do you have a test harness we can run on our infra to compare? We'd like to run identical inputs on our on-prem to measure delta.
[09:01] Priya Raman: Yes — we have a microbenchmark harness that runs with your sample corpus and returns p50/p95/p99, memory profiles, and kv-page statistics. We'll share the repo and a runbook.
[09:13] Jordan Lee: Quick interjection — Ben any security blockers to running the harness?
[09:17] Ben Ortiz: We'll need the harness code and a signed NDA addendum? But generally fine if it's runnable in our VPC with no egress.
[09:25] Priya Raman: We can provide a containerized harness that runs offline, writes results to an S3-compatible bucket in your VPC, or you can have it spit out tar.gz logs we can analyze.
[09:35] Aisha Khan: On chunking strategies: do you recommend overlapping chunks or strict boundaries with rerank? Our docs have sections that cross boundaries often.

[09:42] Priya Raman: Overlap helps with boundary effects, but increases compute. A common approach: chunk with small overlap + a reranker that selects top-k relevant chunks and then stitch with a short compressor or summary tokens. For clinical cross-doc references we also use a graph of mentions to ensure references don't get lost.
[09:58] Carlos Mendes: Does Redwood maintain that graph or is that on the app side?

[10:02] Priya Raman: Either — we provide building blocks in the platform and customers can maintain application-side indexes. For tight control you might keep the index on your side and call into Redwood for model inference.
[10:14] Speaker 6: (mumble) — what about streaming responses with long contexts; do you stream tokens while still loading older KV pages?

[10:20] Priya Raman: We can stream partial responses based on currently-available context. If the request needs far-prefix info we can emit a tentative stream and then patch later — but that creates UX complexity. For deterministic clinical summaries we usually wait until the critical KV pages are loaded before streaming final outputs.

[10:40] Jordan Lee: Alright, let's outline the pilot we discussed: 1) microbenchmark with sample corpus, 2) evaluate 8-bit vs 4-bit on entity recall, 3) test pre-warm using patient ID, 4) run pilot on Dedicated with VPC peering. We'll assign owners in the action items.
[10:58] Aisha Khan: Timeline — we want pilot kick-off in June if possible. Is that realistic?
[11:02] Jordan Lee: Yes — assuming we get sample data and approvals this month, we can kick off a 4–6 week pilot starting early June.
[11:10] Carlos Mendes: Questions from my side: how do you handle model version pinning and rollbacks in Dedicated? It's critical we can pin to a known-good version.
[11:16] Priya Raman: You can pin model versions per route. Rollouts are canary/A-B style and there's a rollback toggle. We also snapshot KV state if you want reproducibility.
[11:28] Ben Ortiz: Regarding logs, will Redwood ever see raw prompts or do we have an option to keep all data in our VPC?

[11:33] Ethan Park: In Private/Data-plane-in-VPC modes, logs and prompts can remain inside the customer VPC; telemetry sent to Redwood control plane is metadata-only unless you opt-in to share logs. We'll provide details in the security pack.
[11:50] Aisha Khan: One more technical: how does sharded KV impact attention computation across devices — do you do cross-GPU all-reduce often?

[11:58] Priya Raman: We minimize cross-GPU all-reduce by sharding KV along sequence/token dimension and aligning attention compute per shard. For attention patterns that require cross-shard contexts we do a staged fetch and local compute to reduce communication. There's no simple free lunch: latency vs parallelism tradeoffs exist and that's where our kernel/runtime heuristics help.
[12:20] Carlos Mendes: Any tips for tokenization at 128k? We have lots of medical shorthand.

[12:25] Priya Raman: Pre-tokenization normalization helps a lot — canonicalize abbreviations, expand measurements, and apply a domain tokenizer if needed. That reduces token bloat and improves recall on entity-level tasks.
[12:38] Speaker 6: Also wonder about cost modeling: do you provide per-token cost estimates that include KV storage and IO?
[12:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, our cost model includes token compute, KV storage, and tiered IO. For Dedicated we can give a fixed commit and expected units/month based on bench runs.
[12:58] Aisha Khan: If we do a pilot, what does success look like? We should define metrics.
[13:03] Carlos Mendes: I'd propose: p95 latency <2s (warm), entity recall >= 0.95 (baseline), and predictable monthly cost within 15% of estimate.
[13:10] Jordan Lee: Good — we'll bake that into the pilot SOW. We'll create a short success criteria doc.

[13:20] Priya Raman: Actionable items from engineering perspective: I need the sample corpus, a list of critical entities, and an infra endpoint for running the harness. We'll run: 1) tokenization pass, 2) 8-bit vs 4-bit eval, 3) pre-warm test, 4) KV eviction stress test.
[13:37] Aisha Khan: We'll get that over. One compliance ask: can you provide a standard data processing addendum?
[13:42] Jordan Lee: Yes — legal will send the DPA and SOC2 artifacts. I'll cc Ben and Lena.
[13:50] Carlos Mendes: Any known limitations we should be worried about?

[13:54] Priya Raman: For extreme scale at 128k+ the main limits are: GPU memory and IO bandwidth for KV page loads, potential quantization regressions on domain-specific NER, and cold-start p99s if you don't pre-warm. Architects should plan pre-warm hooks and evaluation gates.
[14:12] Jordan Lee: We'll include mitigations in the follow-up doc. Ethan — any infra caveats?

[14:16] Ethan Park: Network egress for streaming large KV pages can be heavy — ensure your VPC peering has sufficient bandwidth and consider colocating data plane closer to your storage. Also consider SSD tiers with high IOPS for host-disk tier.
[14:30] Aisha Khan: Good to know. Can the harness measure IO page faults and list top hot pages?
[14:36] Priya Raman: Yes — the harness collects KV-page stats, page fault rates, and provides a heatmap of hot vs cold pages.
[14:46] Speaker 6: (quiet) — any example of the runtime picking different kernels at runtime?

[14:50] Priya Raman: Sure — for shorter sequences it picks flash-attention kernels for maximal throughput; for a 128k prefix with block-sparse retrieval it will pick a blocked kernel that is memory efficient. We'll share profiler traces.

[14:58] Jordan Lee: Alright, wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners. Jordan to share bench CSV, Priya to run microbenchmarks with customer samples, Aisha to provide corpus and constraints, Lena to confirm VPC peering window, Ben to approve NDA addendum. Any final questions?
[15:15] Carlos Mendes: No, that's all. Thanks everyone — appreciate the level of detail.
[15:18] Jordan Lee: Thanks all. We'll follow up with links and schedule the pilot kickoff for first week of June pending approvals.
